statement: The Arrernte (Aranda) subsection system — eight named "skin" categories, an elaboration of the simpler four-section and two-moiety systems found elsewhere in Aboriginal Australia — was formally analyzed by A.R. Radcliffe-Brown, "The Social Organization of Australian Tribes," Oceania 1 (1930-31), which established the "Aranda type" as a named class of kinship system (alongside Kariera-type and Karadjeri-type). Claude Lévi-Strauss, Les structures élémentaires de la parenté (1949; English The Elementary Structures of Kinship, 1969), built his foundational "restricted exchange" vs. "generalized exchange" distinction explicitly on Radcliffe-Brown's typology, with the more complex eight-subsection Aranda system functioning as a paradigm case in the founding text of structuralist kinship theory. This regulates marriage eligibility via classificatory kin categories and is a distinct axis from — not by itself evidence about — who held ceremonial, political, or economic authority.
